title: Church Government — Part 5: One Kind of Elder or Two?
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro
summary: This lesson examines whether Scripture teaches one or two kinds of elders in the local church. Pastor Lyro surveys different historical and denominational views on elder classifications, then demonstrates through careful biblical analysis of 1 Timothy 5:17 and the Greek word "malista" that Scripture teaches a distinction between ruling elders and teaching/preaching elders, both equally essential to church leadership.

transcript:
## Opening Review of Church Government Series

This is our fifth lesson on the subject of church government, where we are asking: what has Christ appointed for his church?

We have studied the concept of authority and submission, seeing what authority is and what submission is. We also examined how good authority works, distinguishing between the authority of counsel and the authority of command. The difference is whether the authority has the ability to force you to obey.

We then surveyed five different models of church government currently used in churches:

1. **Episcopacy (Episcopalian)** — Governed by bishops
2. **Congregationalism** — Ruled by the congregation; however, very few churches actually practice true congregationalism because it requires a congregational vote on everything
3. **Independent Congregationalism** — Each local church is independent and rules itself by elders
4. **Single Pastor Rule** — One pastor rules the church by himself, though no church's bylaws formally state this model
5. **Presbyterianism** — The form of government given to us by God, where each local church is ruled by a plurality of elders

Most importantly, we have established that **Christ is the only head of the church**. There is no other head. Since he is the head, he is the boss, and we should do what he tells us to do.

Last week we examined the terms elders, bishops, and pastors, discovering that they refer to the same office—not different people in the church, but the same group of people. We saw that God appointed a plurality of elders to rule each local congregation.

## Review Quiz on Plurality of Elders

Do you remember the key passage in Acts showing that there are at least two elders in each local church? **Acts 14:23**, where Paul and Barnabas went back to the churches they had established and appointed elders—plural—in each church.

There is also a very important passage in James. **James 5:14** says to call all the elders of the local church—more than one elder.

So we have established that elders are plural, and every local church should have at least two elders.

## The Question: One Kind of Elder or Two?

Now we come to a related question: Are all elders the same, or is there a differentiation within the office of the elder?

## Different Historical Views on Elder Classification

### The Westminster Divines

The Westminster divines—the theologians and scholars present at the assembly that formulated the Westminster Confession and Catechism—identified **three distinct offices or roles** within the eldership:

1. Pastor/Minister
2. Teacher/Doctor
3. Church Governor/Elder

However, Ian Murray, a Scottish Presbyterian and founder of Banner of Truth Trust, argues that though this distinction of minister and ruling elder into separate offices won the day at the assembly, the Scottish members argued differently. The Scottish members contended that ruling elders occupy the **same office** as ministers and are equally presbyters, differing only in their duties. The Scottish members, though only five out of 160 members and unable to vote, were very persuasive in their argument that the word presbyter applies to all elders and they have equal status in the ruling of the church.

### John Calvin

Earlier than the Westminster Assembly, John Calvin taught that there were multiple Christ-appointed offices for the church: ministers, presbyters/elders, teachers, and church governors.

### Charles Hodge (19th Century Princeton)

A major influencer on how American churches practice church government was Charles Hodge, a 19th-century Princeton professor. Hodge found only one office or function in the New Testament to which the term presbyteros (elder) should be related. He argued that:

- The word presbyteros is only used for ministers
- The word bishop is only for ministers
- The word shepherd is always only for ministers

Hodge did **not recognize the divine origin of the office of ruling elder**. Rather, he claimed that ruling elder came into the church through the synagogue as a pragmatic institution that worked well, but is not necessarily appointed and found in the scriptures.

Hodge stated: "There are two classes of officers, the one who both ruled and preached and to whom the scriptures give the titles bishop, presbyteros, pastor, ministers and the other called governments. Who were and use the Latin term seniors, ex plebi delicti, elders chosen from the people to join with the former class in the government of the church. The title bishop or presbyter is never given to any but ministers of the word."

It is very difficult to see this view in the Bible. Also, it is problematic that this important office is taught to be instituted by pragmatism rather than scripture, which does not seem consistent with the scriptures.

### Current Denominational Practice

Today we see different terminology used:

- **Non-Presbyterian churches** use the terms "staff elders" and "non-staff elders" to differentiate between those who get paid and those who don't.
- **Presbyterian denominations** often use the terms "ruling elder and teaching elder" or "minister and ruling elder" to demonstrate the differences in function within the eldership.

There is broad acknowledgement that there is some distinction in the office of the elder, no matter how you describe your position.

**The Bible Presbyterian Church** states that the ordinary and perpetual officers in the church are: ministers, ruling elders, and deacons.

**The Orthodox Presbyterian Church (OPC)** uses similar language: "The ordinary and perpetual offices in the church are those given for the ministry of the word of God, of rule and of mercy. Those who share in the rule of the church may be called elders or presbyters, bishops or church governors. Those administering mercy and service are called deacons. Those elders who have been edged and called of Christ to labor also in the word and teaching are called ministers."

**The Presbyterian Church in America (PCA)** uses the language of "teaching elder" and "ruling elder" in their government documents, formally calling pastors "teaching elders" and other elders "ruling elders."

## What Does the Bible Say?

No matter how you label it or how many offices you describe, there is no church in the Presbyterian world that practices 100% equality between the minister and the ruling elder. At the very least, there must be a distinction in function if not in office.

A helpful illustration is the military. If you're enlisted as an E7, there may be thousands of E7s. Not every E7 is doing the same thing. They have different duties, and sometimes an E7 may be elevated over other E7s because of the function being exercised. Similarly, in the church, every elder is an "E7"—they all have equal status and authority—but they exercise different functions.

Last week we saw that the terms bishop, elder, and pastor (or shepherd) are used interchangeably. They are not titles of separate offices; rather, they describe functions of a single office. Yet the scriptures teach that the term presbyteros (elder) describes **two classes of elders**. They are all elders, but there are two classes.

David Dixon, a 19th-century Scottish Presbyterian ruling elder, recognized this distinction: "There is only one distinction, that between the elder who labors in word and doctrine—the pastor of the flock—and what are called the lay elders who rule."

## The Key: 1 Timothy 5:17

The clearest place we see this distinction is in **1 Timothy 5:17**:

> "Let the elders who rule well be counted worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in the word and doctrine."

In this verse, Paul singles out those who labor in preaching and teaching from among the elders who rule well, thereby creating a duality in the office. You have all these elders who rule well, and from within that group, there are some who also labor in word and doctrine.

The key to understanding this is the word **"especially"**—the Greek word **malista**. This word singles out a **subgroup from a whole group**. All members of the subgroup are part of the whole group, but the subgroup has additional characteristics.

## Understanding the Greek Word "Malista"

The word malista is used only 11-12 times in the entire New Testament, with 8 times directly from Paul's pen. Let us examine six passages to understand how this word functions:

### Galatians 6:10

> "Let us do good to all people, especially to those who belong to the family of believers."

The big group is "everyone." The subgroup is "the household of faith." Paul is emphasizing that the household of faith is a subcategory that requires special attention.

### Philippians 4:22

> "All the saints send you greetings, especially those who belong to Caesar's household."

The big category is "all the saints." The subcategory is "those saints that are also part of Caesar's household." This characteristic is not shared by all the saints.

### 1 Timothy 4:10

> "For to this end we both labor and suffer reproach, because we trust in the living God, who is the Savior of all men, especially of those who believe."

The big group is "all men." Christ is the Savior of all men; there is no other Savior. But there is a special relationship of Christ with a subset of all people—those who believe.

### 1 Timothy 5:8

> "But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever."

The big group is "relatives." The subgroup is "his household"—the immediate family that lives with him. All relatives do not necessarily live with him, but he is responsible to help those that do.

### 2 Timothy 4:13

> "When you come, bring the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, and my books, especially the parchments."

The big group is "books" that Paul loved. If Timothy cannot bring them all, "especially the parchments" are the ones Paul really wants.

### Titus 1:10-11

> "For there are many insubordinate, both idle and talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision."

The big group is "many insubordinate, both idle and talkers and deceivers." The subgroup is "Jewish people who are doing that."

## Applying Malista to 1 Timothy 5:17

Now let us apply what we have learned to **1 Timothy 5:17**:

> "Let the elders who rule well be counted worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in the word and doctrine."

**The big group:** Elders who rule well.

**The subgroup:** Those who labor in word and doctrine.

Those who labor in word and doctrine are also ruling. They share that characteristic with the big group, but they also have something else they are supposed to do—labor in word and doctrine.

## Two Categories of Elders

This teaches us there are **two categories of elders**:

1. Those who rule
2. Those who rule and labor in word and doctrine

**All elders rule.** No matter what your title—pastor or ruling elder—your role is to rule. When the session (the elders of the local church) meets, there is parity. Everyone has the same voice in voting. There is no one elder who has more power to vote than another. When we meet as a presbytery, everyone has the same saying, the same power, the same discussion, and the same duties.

**The only difference is when the minister labors in word and doctrine.** That is where the distinction lies. The preaching and teaching elders are commonly referred to as pastors in the modern church.

This also tells us that **not all elders are called to teach and preach publicly in the church.** Especially those who labor in word and doctrine—those are the ones called to teach and preach publicly in the church. All elders are called to rule. Some elders are called to preach and teach publicly in the church.

## The Qualification: "Able to Teach" in 1 Timothy 3:2

A question arises: In **1 Timothy 3:2**, we see that elders must be "able to teach." How is this qualification different from those who "labor in preaching and teaching"?

In **1 Timothy 3:2**, Paul provides a list of qualifications for the elder:

> "Therefore a bishop must be blameless, the husband of one wife, temperate, sober-minded, of good behavior, hospitable, able to teach."

The word "able to teach" is used only twice in the entire New Testament. This word can mean both "able to teach" and "teachable." It is a difficult word to define precisely.

David Dixon, the 19th-century Scottish Presbyterian elder, suggests that the general qualification of being "able to teach" means that **every elder must have good knowledge of the Bible and be able to communicate that knowledge in a way that is beneficial to those who hear him**.

Paul clarifies what it means to be "able to teach" in his instructions to Titus in **Titus 1:9**:

> "Holding fast the faithful word as he has been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and convict those who contradict."

This describes one-on-one ministry. **Being "able to teach" means being able to engage people in conversation, to exhort and to convict those who contradict.** Every elder must know the doctrine of the church well enough that he can effectively defend it.

**Not every elder is called to preach or teach publicly.** Tim Whitmer, author of *The Shepherd Leader*, distinguishes that being "able to teach" means that every elder should be able to:

- Disciple people
- Mentor people
- Counsel people
- Refute heresy

This is different than the public ministry of the word on the Lord's Day in the church. All ruling elders possess this ability to teach in one-on-one settings. Some ruling elders are additionally called to preach and teach publicly to the congregation.

## Conclusion: God's Design for Elder Leadership

The scriptures teach that **a plurality of biblically qualified elders is God's way to shepherd his flock**.

- **All elders who shepherd the flock of God** in each local church will rule well. That is the calling they have.
- **Some will rule well and labor in preaching and teaching.**
- **Both kinds of elders are God's gifts to his church** and should be present in every local church.

## Preview of Next Lesson

It is not enough that a church has a plurality of elders. These elders must be qualified according to God's Word. That is what we will start looking at next Lord's Day.
